We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{3}{4}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{e}^{x}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{-1}-{e}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot (\frac{1}{e}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14260591/assets/4af4a2b7389d3773cc71e843190c6ab111355248a15e6165a8e39e37252061b9.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{3}{4}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot (\frac{1}{e}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(\frac{1}{e}-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{4e}.\end{aligned}
$$
